citation: Plotkin DL, Rodas MA, Vigotsky AD, McIntosh MC, Breeze E, Ubrik R, Robitzsch C, Agyin-Birikorang A, Mattingly ML, Michel JM, Kontos NJ, Lennon S, Fruge AD, Wilburn CM, Weimar WH, Bashir A, Beyers RJ, Henselmans M, Contreras BM, Roberts MD. Hip thrust and back squat training elicit similar gluteus muscle hypertrophy and transfer similarly to the deadlift. Front Physiol. 2023;14:1279170
design: Randomised parallel-group trial, set-volume equated, supervised
intervention_comparison: Barbell hip thrust only vs barbell back squat only (as deep as possible); set volume equated
outcome_measure: MRI muscle CSA (gluteus max lower/mid/upper, glute med+min, quadriceps, adductors, hamstrings); 3RM squat, hip thrust, deadlift; isometric wall push
result_effect_uncertainty: Between-group estimates, (-) favours hip thrust, (+) favours squat, effect +/- SE [95% CI]: lower glute max -1.6 +/- 2.1 cm2 [-6.1, 2.0]; mid -0.5 +/- 1.7 [-4.0, 2.6]; upper -0.5 +/- 2.6 [-5.8, 4.1]; glute med+min -1.8 +/- 1.5 [-4.6, 1.4]; hamstrings 0.1 +/- 0.6 [-0.9, 1.4] (little or no growth in either group); quadriceps +3.6 +/- 1.5 [0.7, 6.4] and adductors +2.5 +/- 0.7 [1.2, 3.9] favour squat. Squat 3RM +14 +/- 2 kg [9, 18] favours squat; hip thrust 3RM -26 +/- 5 kg [-34, -16] favours hip thrust; deadlift 3RM 0 +/- 2 kg [-4, 3]; wall push -7 +/- 12 N [-32, 17]. First-session EMG was higher in hip thrust but did not predict growth
limitations_coi: Untrained only; 9 wk; CIs for glutes are wide (cannot rule out a few cm2 either way); authors note prone MRI positioning may compress glutes. COI: co-authors Contreras (BC Strength, sells hip thrust equipment) and Henselmans sell exercise products; gift funds partly from them. 2026 correction adds that BC Strength donated the hip thrust apparatus and that the trial was registered only retrospectively; journal judged findings not unreliable
verification: PubMed PMID 37877099 abstract; Europe PMC full text PMC10593473 (abstract, limitations); Crossref DOI resolves 2026-11-16, updated-by correction 10.3389/fphys.2026.1987823 (read in full via PMC13752533: funding/COI/registration only, no data change)

design: Two-group training study (allocation method not stated in abstract)
intervention_comparison: Back squat only vs hip thrust only; 1 session/wk, 6 sets/wk per Krause Neto 2025 table (SECONDARY)
outcome_measure: Ultrasound muscle thickness (quadriceps, gluteus maximus); 1RM squat and hip thrust

limitations_coi: TRUST FLAG: four other papers from this first author/group are retracted (verified today in PubMed: PMIDs 31188644, 31072272, 30779716, 29781936). citation: Barbalho M, Souza D, Coswig V, Abrahin O, Paoli A, Gentil P. The Effects of Resistance Exercise Selection on Muscle Size and Strength in Trained Women. Int J Sports Med. 2021;42(4):371-376

citation: Kubo K, Ikebukuro T, Yata H. Effects of squat training with different depths on lower limb muscle volumes. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2019;119(9):1933-1942
population: Young men (training status not stated in abstract)

outcome_measure: MRI muscle volume (knee extensors, rectus femoris, hamstrings, adductors, gluteus maximus); 1RM full and half squat

citation: Kassiano W, Costa B, Kunevaliki G, Lisboa F, Prado A, Alves L, Tricoli I, Stavinski N, Francsuel J, Cyrino ES. Comparison of Muscle Hypertrophy and Strength Adaptations Induced by Back Squat and Leg Extension Resistance Exercises. J Strength Cond Res. 2026;40(4):367-376

citation: Zabaleta-Korta A, Fernandez-Pena E, Torres-Unda J, Garbisu-Hualde A, Santos-Concejero J. The role of exercise selection in regional Muscle Hypertrophy: A randomized controlled trial. J Sports Sci. 2021;39(20):2298-2304

citation: Kassiano W, Costa B, Kunevaliki G, Soares D, Zacarias G, Manske I, Takaki Y, Ruggiero MF, Stavinski N, Francsuel J, Tricoli I, Carneiro MAS, Cyrino ES. population: Young women (training status not stated in abstract)
intervention_comparison: Calf raise on a horizontal leg press: full ROM (-25 to +25 deg) vs bottom-half partials (-25 to 0 deg) vs top-half partials (0 to +25 deg); 3 sets of 15-20RM
outcome_measure: Ultrasound thickness of medial and lateral gastrocnemius
result_effect_uncertainty: Medial gastrocnemius: bottom-half +15.2% vs full +6.7% vs top-half +3.4% (p<=0.009 for bottom-half vs each). Lateral gastrocnemius: bottom-half +14.9% vs top-half +6.2% (p<0.024); vs full +7.3% p=0.060
limitations_coi: Young women; 8 wk; thickness; about 14 per group; already covered as a ROM study in the repo's top-5 work - included here because it changes how to do the calf raise
verification: PubMed PMID 37015016 abstract; Crossref DOI resolves 2026-11-16, no retraction/correction in update-to/updated-by

citation: Nunes JP, Costa BDV, Kassiano W, Kunevaliki G, Castro-E-Souza P, Rodacki ALF, Fortes LS, Cyrino ES. Different Foot Positioning During Calf Training to Induce Portion-Specific Gastrocnemius Muscle Hypertrophy. J Strength Cond Res. 2020;34(8):2347-2351
design: Randomised trial with legs as units (within-subject element)
population: Young men (23 +/- 4 y); training status not stated in abstract
intervention_comparison: Unilateral calf raise on a horizontal leg press with foot pointed outward vs inward vs forward; 3-4 sets of 20-25 reps
outcome_measure: Ultrasound thickness of medial and lateral gastrocnemius
result_effect_uncertainty: Medial head: outward +8.4%, inward +3.8%, forward +5.8%. Lateral head: outward +5.5%, inward +9.1%, forward +6.4%. Outward vs inward differed significantly (p<0.05)
limitations_coi: Small differences (a few %) on single-site ultrasound thickness; about 14-15 legs per condition; not replicated; abstract only
verification: PubMed PMID 32735428 abstract; Crossref DOI resolves 2026-11-16, no retraction/correction in update-to/updated-by

citation: Larsen S, Sandberg NO, Schoenfeld BJ, Fredriksen AB, Kristiansen BS, Wolf M, van den Tillaar R, Swinton PA, Falch HN. Resistance Training Beyond Momentary Failure: The Effects of Past-Failure Partials Versus Initial Partials on Calf Muscle Hypertrophy Among a Resistance-Trained Cohort. Eur J Sport Sci. 2025;25(9):e70030
intervention_comparison: Unilateral Smith machine calf raise, 4 sets to failure: bottom-range (lengthened) partials only vs full ROM followed by past-failure partials
outcome_measure: Ultrasound thickness of medial gastrocnemius
result_effect_uncertainty: Average treatment effect favouring bottom-range partials: 0.40 mm (95% credible interval -0.06 to 0.85 mm); p(>0)=0.958; Bayes factor 1.2 ('anecdotal'). Both conditions produced medium-to-large within-condition growth
limitations_coi: Uncertain difference (interval includes zero); 8 wk; within-subject; full text (PMC12375417) not read

citation: Hernandez-Belmonte A, Martinez-Cava A, Buendia-Romero A, Franco-Lopez F, Pallares JG. Free-Weight and Machine-Based Training Are Equally Effective on Strength and Hypertrophy: Challenging a Traditional Myth. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2023;55(12):2316-2327
design: Two-group training trial, identical training variables (allocation method not stated in abstract)
intervention_comparison: Free-weight vs machine versions of full squat, bench press, prone bench pull, shoulder press; velocity-based load control
outcome_measure: Ultrasound CSA of quadriceps (proximal, distal), pectoralis major, rectus abdominis; relative 1RM and velocity vs low/high loads in 8 tests (4 exercises x 2 modalities); joint discomfort (WOMAC, DASH)
result_effect_uncertainty: All muscle CSAs increased in both groups, no significant between-group difference (difference in % change <=2.0%, P>=0.208). Strength across the 8 tests similar (difference <=1.8%, P>=0.216), but each group gained most in the modality it trained. Joint discomfort fell in both groups (P>=0.144 between groups). Rectus abdominis CSA increased although the abstract lists no direct ab exercise among the four trained lifts
limitations_coi: 8 wk; n=19 per group cannot exclude small differences; no CIs in abstract; no ab-training comparison arm, so the rectus abdominis result is not a test of direct ab work
verification: PubMed PMID 37535335 abstract; Crossref DOI resolves 2026-11-16, no retraction/correction in update-to/updated-by

citation: Haugen ME, Varvik FT, Larsen S, Haugen AS, van den Tillaar R, Bjornsen T. Effect of free-weight vs. machine-based strength training on maximal strength, hypertrophy and jump performance - a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Sports Sci Med Rehabil. 2023;15(1):103
design: Systematic review + meta-analysis (PRISMA), direct comparisons of >=6 wk
intervention_comparison: Free-weight vs machine-based strength training
outcome_measure: Maximal dynamic and isometric strength, countermovement jump, hypertrophy
result_effect_uncertainty: Hypertrophy SMD -0.055 (95% CI -0.397 to 0.287; p=0.751). Strength tested with free weights: SMD -0.210 (-0.391 to -0.029; p=0.023) favouring free-weight training. Strength tested on machines: SMD 0.291 (-0.017 to 0.600; p=0.064) tending to favour machine training. Direct comparison dynamic strength 0.084 (-0.106 to 0.273); isometric -0.079 (-0.432 to 0.273); jump -0.209 (-0.597 to 0.179)
limitations_coi: Only 5 hypertrophy studies, several with weak measures (circumference, skinfold, Bod Pod); pre-post correlation taken from a single study; no funding; no conflicts declared
verification: PubMed PMID 37582807 abstract; Europe PMC full text PMC10426227 (methods, study table, funding); Crossref DOI resolves 2026-11-16, no update notices

citation: Heidel KA, Novak ZJ, Dankel SJ. Machines and free weight exercises: a systematic review and meta-analysis comparing changes in muscle size, strength, and power. J Sports Med Phys Fitness. 2022;62(8):1061-1070
n: Not stated in abstract (3 hypertrophy studies per Haugen 2023; SECONDARY)
intervention_comparison: Free-weight vs machine-based training
outcome_measure: Strength (free-weight test, machine test, neutral test), power, hypertrophy
result_effect_uncertainty: Free-weight-tested strength favours free-weight training ES 0.655 (95% CI 0.269 to 1.041). Machine-tested strength favours machine training ES -0.784 (-1.223 to -0.344). Neutral-device strength ES 0.128 (-0.303 to 0.559). Power ES -0.049 (-0.557 to 0.460). Hypertrophy ES -0.01 (-0.525 to 0.545) as printed
limitations_coi: Hypertrophy CI as printed in the abstract is not centred on the point estimate (likely a typo: +0.01 or lower bound mis-signed) - do not over-read it; very few hypertrophy studies; abstract only
verification: PubMed PMID 34609100 abstract; Crossref DOI resolves 2026-11-16, no retraction/correction in update-to/updated-by

citation: Schwanbeck SR, Cornish SM, Barss T, Chilibeck PD. Effects of Training With Free Weights Versus Machines on Muscle Mass, Strength, Free Testosterone, and Free Cortisol Levels. J Strength Cond Res. 2020;34(7):1851-1859
population: Young adults (22 +/- 3 y); training status not stated in abstract
duration: 8 wk, each muscle 2-3x/wk, 3-4 sets of 4-10 reps
intervention_comparison: Free-weight programme vs machine programme
outcome_measure: Ultrasound thickness of biceps and quadriceps; free-weight bench and squat, Smith squat, machine bench strength; salivary hormones
result_effect_uncertainty: Biceps and quadriceps thickness increased (p<0.01) with no difference between groups. Machine bench press strength rose more in machine group (13.9% vs 8.6%, interaction p=0.05). Free-weight bench, free-weight squat and Smith squat strength rose 11-19% in both with no group difference
limitations_coi: 8 wk; no effect sizes/CIs in abstract; acute testosterone difference is not a training outcome
verification: PubMed PMID 32358310 abstract; Crossref DOI resolves 2026-11-16, no retraction/correction in update-to/updated-by

citation: Marcos-Frutos D, Miras-Moreno S, Marquez G, Garcia-Ramos A. Comparative Effects of the Free Weights and Smith Machine Squat and Bench Press: The Important Role of Specificity for Strength Adaptations. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2025;20(2):292-300
design: Two-group trial, balanced by sex and relative strength
intervention_comparison: Free-weight vs Smith machine back squat and bench press; 4 sets at 70% 1RM, 20-25% velocity loss
outcome_measure: CSA of vastus lateralis and pectoralis major; load-velocity profile (load-axis intercept as strength estimate) in both modalities; bench reps to failure
result_effect_uncertainty: Vastus lateralis and pectoralis major CSA improved comparably in both groups. Strength (load-axis intercept) improved more when the test matched the training modality
limitations_coi: No numbers in abstract; students; 8 wk; moderate effort (not to failure)
verification: PubMed PMID 39740659 abstract; Crossref DOI resolves 2026-11-16, no retraction/correction in update-to/updated-by

citation: Kassiano W, Nunes JP, Costa B, Ribeiro AS, Schoenfeld BJ, Cyrino ES. Does Varying Resistance Exercises Promote Superior Muscle Hypertrophy and Strength Gains? A Systematic Review. J Strength Cond Res. 2022;36(6):1753-1762
intervention_comparison: Varied vs fixed exercise selection
outcome_measure: Muscle hypertrophy, strength
result_effect_uncertainty: Qualitative: some systematic variation seems to help regional hypertrophy and dynamic strength; excessive or random rotation may compromise gains; redundant exercises add nothing. No pooled estimate
limitations_coi: Narrative synthesis of 8 small studies in men; no effect size; authors overlap with primary studies
verification: PubMed PMID 35438660 abstract; Crossref DOI resolves 2026-11-16, no retraction/correction in update-to/updated-by

citation: Fonseca RM, Roschel H, Tricoli V, de Souza EO, Wilson JM, Laurentino GC, Aihara AY, de Souza Leao AR, Ugrinowitsch C. Changes in exercises are more effective than in loading schemes to improve muscle strength. J Strength Cond Res. 2014;28(11):3085-3092
design: Randomised controlled trial, 4 training groups + control
intervention_comparison: Constant vs varied lower-body exercise, crossed with constant vs varied intensity (constant-exercise groups did squat only per Baz-Valle 2019; SECONDARY)
outcome_measure: MRI CSA of whole quadriceps and each head; squat 1RM
result_effect_uncertainty: Whole-quadriceps CSA rose similarly in all training groups (9.3% to 12.2%). Varied-exercise groups grew all four quadriceps heads; constant-exercise groups did not significantly grow vastus medialis and/or rectus femoris (p>0.05). Constant-intensity varied-exercise group had the largest squat strength gain (effect-size confidence limits of the difference vs the other groups 0.59 to 2.28)
limitations_coi: About 10 per group; 'no significant growth' in a head within a small group is not proof of a between-group difference; not resistance-trained lifters; abstract only
verification: PubMed PMID 24832974 abstract; Crossref DOI resolves 2026-11-16, no retraction/correction in update-to/updated-by

citation: Baz-Valle E, Schoenfeld BJ, Torres-Unda J, Santos-Concejero J, Balsalobre-Fernandez C. The effects of exercise variation in muscle thickness, maximal strength and motivation in resistance trained men. PLoS One. 2019;14(12):e0226989
intervention_comparison: Fixed exercises (back squat, deadlift, leg press, hip thrust, leg extension, leg curl...) vs exercises randomly drawn each session by an app from an 80-exercise database; 3 sets x 6 exercises
outcome_measure: Ultrasound thickness of vastus lateralis, rectus femoris, vastus intermedius; 1RM back squat and bench press; intrinsic motivation
result_effect_uncertainty: Both groups: large significant gains in squat and bench 1RM and in vastus lateralis and rectus femoris thickness, no between-group differences. Vastus intermedius increased significantly only in the fixed group. Motivation improved moderately only in the random group
limitations_coi: n=19 completers: cannot detect small differences; rep ranges were also randomised in the experimental group (confound); single-site thickness; authors declare no competing interests
verification: PubMed PMID 31881066 abstract; Europe PMC full text PMC6934277 (methods, limitations, competing interests); Crossref DOI resolves 2026-11-16, no update notices

citation: Costa BDV, Kassiano W, Nunes JP, Kunevaliki G, Castro-E-Souza P, Rodacki A, Cyrino LT, Cyrino ES, Fortes LS. Does Performing Different Resistance Exercises for the Same Muscle Group Induce Non-homogeneous Hypertrophy? Int J Sports Med. 2021;42(9):803-811
intervention_comparison: Same exercises every session vs different exercises for the same muscle group across sessions
outcome_measure: Ultrasound thickness at proximal, middle, distal sites of lateral and anterior thigh, elbow flexors and extensors
result_effect_uncertainty: Varied group increased thickness at all sites (P<0.05). Non-varied group did not significantly increase the middle lateral thigh or the proximal elbow flexors (P>0.05). Abstract gives no between-group effect sizes
limitations_coi: n=11 per group; within-group significance only; detrained men; abstract only
verification: PubMed PMID 33440446 abstract; Crossref DOI resolves 2026-11-16, no retraction/correction in update-to/updated-by

citation: Rauch JT, Ugrinowitsch C, Barakat CI, Alvarez MR, Brummert DL, Aube DW, Barsuhn AS, Hayes D, Tricoli V, De Souza EO. Auto-Regulated Exercise Selection Training Regimen Produces Small Increases in Lean Body Mass and Maximal Strength Adaptations in Strength-trained Individuals. J Strength Cond Res. 2020;34(4):1133-1140
population: Strength-trained men (squat 1.87x and bench 1.38x body mass)
intervention_comparison: Self-selected exercises each session vs fixed exercise selection
outcome_measure: DXA lean body mass; 1RM back squat and bench press
result_effect_uncertainty: Lean body mass: self-selected +2.47% (ES 0.35; 95% CI of change 0.030 to 3.197 kg) vs fixed +1.37% (ES 0.21; -0.500 to 2.475 kg). Bench 1RM +6.48% vs +5.14%. Squat 1RM +9.55% vs +11.54% (similar). Self-selected group lifted more total volume load (573,288 vs 464,600 kg, p=0.024)

citation: Kassiano W, Costa B, Kunevaliki G, Nunes JP, Castro-E-Souza P, de Paula Felipe J, Tricoli I, Luiz A, Tricoli V, Cyrino ES. Muscle Hypertrophy and Strength Adaptations to Systematically Varying Resistance Exercises. Res Q Exerc Sport. 2025;96(2):371-381
design: Randomised controlled trial, two groups, sets equated
population: Young women (training status not stated in abstract)
intervention_comparison: Constant: 45-degree leg press + stiff-leg deadlift every session. Varied: leg press + stiff-leg deadlift (day 1), hack squat + prone leg curl (day 2), Smith squat + seated leg curl (day 3). 2 sets of 10-15RM per exercise
outcome_measure: Ultrasound thickness of anterior, lateral, posterior thigh at proximal-to-distal sites; 1RM 45-degree leg press and leg extension (untrained exercise)
result_effect_uncertainty: Thickness rose similarly at all muscles and sites: constant +7.8% to +17.7% vs varied +7.5% to +19.3% (p>0.05). 1RM rose similarly: constant +24.4% to +32.1% vs varied +29.0% to +30.1% (p>0.05)
limitations_coi: Young women, likely untrained; only 2 sets per exercise; 10 wk; no CIs in abstract; largest trial on variety but not trained lifters
verification: PubMed PMID 39388663 abstract; Crossref DOI resolves 2026-11-16, no retraction/correction in update-to/updated-by

citation: Varovic D, Wolf M, Schoenfeld BJ, Steele J, Grgic J, Mikulic P. Does Muscle Length Influence Regional Hypertrophy? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Int J Sports Med. 2025;46(14):1027-1036
intervention_comparison: Training at longer vs shorter mean muscle length (via ROM or exercise selection)
outcome_measure: Regional hypertrophy at proximal (25%), mid (50%), distal (75%) sites
result_effect_uncertainty: Longer vs shorter muscle length: proximal SMD 0.05 (95% quantile interval -0.07 to 0.16); mid 0.07 (-0.02 to 0.15); distal 0.09 (-0.01 to 0.19); as % 0.57% (-1.92 to 3.24), 1.22% (-0.77 to 3.22), 1.88% (-0.44 to 4.34). Trivial differences, slight trend toward more distal growth at longer lengths
limitations_coi: Conditions differed by only 21.8% of mean muscle length on average, so big contrasts (e.g. seated vs prone curl) may be diluted; not lower-body only; abstract only
verification: PubMed PMID 40570881 abstract; Crossref DOI resolves 2026-11-16, no retraction/correction in update-to/updated-by

citation: Saeterbakken AH, Stien N, Paulsen G, Behm DG, Andersen V, Solstad TEJ, Prieske O. Task Specificity of Dynamic Resistance Training and Its Transferability to Non-trained Isometric Muscle Strength: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis. Sports Med. 2025;55(7):1651-1676
population: Healthy adults 16-60 y, trained and untrained
intervention_comparison: Dynamic resistance training; tested on the trained dynamic lift vs an untrained isometric test
outcome_measure: Dynamic (trained-task) strength vs isometric (untrained-task) strength
result_effect_uncertainty: Trained dynamic strength SMD 0.98 (95% CI 0.91 to 1.06) vs untrained isometric strength SMD 0.42 (0.35 to 0.49): about twice the effect on the trained task. Hypertrophy did not predict either strength change (p>=0.222)
limitations_coi: Within-group pre-post SMDs; dynamic-vs-isometric is only one kind of specificity; not lower-body only; full text (PMC12296774) not read
verification: PubMed PMID 40314751 abstract; Crossref DOI resolves 2026-11-16, no retraction/correction in update-to/updated-by
